fixes.explanation: That's the reason in the same breath. The LORD says, “Make him drunk, because he has magnified himself against the LORD…” (Jeremiah 48:26). To magnify yourself is to make yourself big, and here it's aimed straight at the LORD. Moab is the one doing it.

I'd love to tell you about a treaty, but this passage doesn't say a word about Egypt or any agreement. The reason is right there in verse 26: Moab “…has magnified himself against the LORD…” That's the whole reason given. I once searched the whole bakery for my timer, and it was sitting right under my hat.
A refuge is a safe place, and the verse says nothing like that for Moab. It says Moab “…will also become a laughingstock.” (Jeremiah 48:26). Laughingstock is the word the verse gives.

Right. The LORD says, “I have stopped the flow of wine from the presses; no one treads them with shouts of joy…” (Jeremiah 48:33). The joy is gone from the shouting. The verse even says, “…their shouts are not for joy.”
Meribah isn't a name this passage uses. The verse says, “for even the waters of Nimrim have dried up.” (Jeremiah 48:34). Nimrim is the name to hold onto here.

Marah isn't named in this passage. Verse 34 says, “for even the waters of Nimrim have dried up.” Nimrim is the one that goes with this cry across Moab. A good guess, friend, just point it at the right water.

Yes, verse 36 says the LORD's heart laments for the men of Kir-heres, “…because the wealth they acquired has perished.” The verse says His heart laments like a flute. I think that's a tender way to say it.
Walls aren't in this verse at all. The reason given is, “…because the wealth they acquired has perished.” (Jeremiah 48:36). It's about wealth, not building projects.

A stone tablet is a different picture, friend. The verse says the LORD shattered Moab “…like an unwanted jar…” (Jeremiah 48:38). A jar is the image here. Everyone on the rooftops and in the public squares is mourning.

A raven sounds dramatic, but the verse picks another bird. It says, “Behold, an eagle swoops down and spreads his wings against Moab.” (Jeremiah 48:40). The eagle is the one doing the swooping. Nice try, friend.

A lion is a different picture, friend. The verse says their hearts will be “…like the heart of a woman in labor.” (Jeremiah 48:41). That's after Kirioth is taken and the strongholds are seized. I think it shows how shaken they are.
That's the word. Verse 46 says, “…your sons have been taken into exile and your daughters have gone into captivity.” Exile means being taken away from home.
Battle isn't the word the verse uses. It says, “…your sons have been taken into exile and your daughters have gone into captivity.” (Jeremiah 48:46). Exile means being taken away from home.

Hiding is a different picture from this verse. It says, “…your sons have been taken into exile and your daughters have gone into captivity.” (Jeremiah 48:46). That's being taken away, not tucking yourself out of sight.

Hold on, friend, because the last verse adds something. The LORD says, “Yet in the latter days I will restore Moab from captivity…” (Jeremiah 48:47). Right after that comes “Here ends the judgment on Moab.”
